messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Nadia is a 34-year-old agricultural worker who came to therapy at the urging of her sister, after months of increasingly rigid routines and a growing sense that she was becoming unrecognisable to herself. She had been divorced for three years, living alone in a small apartment near the fields where she worked, and she described her life as “a series of tasks I have to get through.” What had brought her to the point of seeking help was a recent morning when she had scrubbed her kitchen counters for nearly two hours before leaving for work, then arrived late and found herself unable to stop watching the other workers’ hands, certain that someone was about to do something dangerous.

The event that had set everything in motion occurred two years earlier, in the packing shed where Nadia had worked for nearly a decade. She had been sorting tomatoes when a man she knew only by face—a seasonal worker who had been quiet and kept to himself—began shouting. In the moments that followed, Nadia watched as he pulled a knife and attacked a supervisor who had fired him the day before. The violence was brief but brutal, and Nadia stood frozen, unable to move or look away, as the supervisor bled onto the concrete floor. Other workers screamed and ran; someone called 911. The man was arrested, the supervisor survived, but Nadia never returned to the packing shed. She requested a transfer to the fields, where she worked alone, walking rows of crops, far from the building where she could still see, in her mind, the exact angle of the knife and the colour of the blood spreading across the grey floor.

In the months that followed, Nadia found herself unable to tolerate certain conversations. If a coworker mentioned a disagreement with a family member or described a conflict at a store, she would walk away midsentence, her heart pounding. She had come to believe that people were not what they seemed—that anyone could become dangerous without warning, and that the calm surface of a person’s face could hide something violent underneath. This distrust extended to everyone, even her sister, whom she loved. When her sister tried to talk about the event, Nadia would say, “I only think about good things now,” and change the subject. She had decided that if she forced herself to think only positive thoughts, she could keep the bad ones at bay. But the positive thoughts felt thin and unconvincing, like paper laid over a hole.

Babies had become unbearable. The sound of an infant crying—even from a passing car or a television in a waiting room—sent a cold wave through her body. She had no children of her own, but the sound felt like a signal of something helpless and unprotected, and it made her want to run. She had stopped visiting her sister’s home because her sister had a toddler, and the sound of the child’s voice, even when happy, made her chest tighten. She told her sister she was busy with work.

At home, Nadia cleaned. She scrubbed her small apartment every evening, often into the night, arranging and rearranging the few objects she owned. She was not cleaning because she thought the apartment was dirty; she was cleaning because the act of ordering her surroundings was the only thing that made her feel, briefly, that she was in control of something. When a thought about the attack intruded—and they intruded many times a day, unbidden, vivid—she would try to push it out of her mind, sometimes by saying “no” aloud, sometimes by starting a new task. But the thoughts always came back, and the effort of pushing them left her exhausted.

Nadia had come to feel that she no longer belonged anywhere. She did not belong in the fields, because the other workers talked about their lives and she could not join in. She did not belong with her family, because she could not explain why she avoided them. She did not belong in her own life, because the person she had been—someone who laughed easily, who trusted her coworkers, who believed that hard work led to safety—had disappeared. She had lost her faith in people, in the idea that the world was predictable, in any higher power that would have allowed what she saw to happen. She no longer prayed, though she had prayed every night before.

What finally brought Nadia to therapy was a panic attack in the field. A tractor backfired, and she dropped to her knees, shaking, convinced that a gun had gone off. Her supervisor found her there and told her to go home. She sat in her apartment that evening, looking at the clean counters, the arranged cabinets, the silent rooms, and she thought: I cannot keep doing this alone. She told her therapist in the first session that she was afraid of two things: that she would never feel safe again, and that she would never feel like herself again. She was not sure which frightened her more.
